title: Same Context, Different Agents: A Behavioral Study of SemanticLayers, Orchestration and Compaction in Data Agents

paper.title: Same Context, Different Agents: A Behavioral Study of Semantic Layers, Orchestration and Compaction in Data Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Answering questions over heterogeneous data means combining evidence from files, databases, documents and the web. Data agents automate this, but their success depends on context. Three context-engineering techniques (CETs) help by shaping it: semantic layers describe the data, orchestration splits work among agents, and compaction condenses interaction history. Existing studies validate each CET alone, leaving open how agent behavior shapes its effect. We present a comprehensive analysis of the three CETs, alone and combined, with seven large language models (LLMs) on 1,514 long-horizon tasks from five benchmarks, covering behavior, accuracy and cost. We find that data agents without CETs form three behavior groups: investigators, premature answerers that answer without inspecting data, and early stoppers that give up. Each CET delivers its known benefit, from more investigation to smaller prompts, but only the behavior group it matches turns that benefit into accuracy, such as premature answerers under orchestration. For investigators, the same CETs can hurt: the semantic layer stops them from looking, orchestration makes them overconfident, costing 5 percentage points, and compaction makes them repeat steps. Combining CETs yields smaller gains and losses than their sum. We derive guidance for choosing CETs by agent behavior, task demands and accuracy-cost trade-offs.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The goal of data analysis is to turn raw data into answers. Analysts start from a question but must find the relevant sources among many files, tables, documents and web pages ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , read data that is heterogeneous across and within sources, with irregular layouts, entity names in multiple languages, obfuscated columns and metrics defined elsewhere ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Lei et al., 2025 ) , align it and compute a result. Agents built on large language models (LLMs) that reason and act with tools ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) are increasingly applied to this problem ( Hong et al., 2025 ; Jing et al., 2025 ) and complete ever longer tasks ( Kwa et al., 2025 ) , yet they remain unreliable ( Jing et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) . Much of the difficulty comes from the model’s context. The data is too large to show in full, so the agent must decide what to look at; its history grows with every step; and models use long inputs unevenly, overlooking information in the middle of a long prompt and degrading as it grows even when it holds what they need ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2025 ) . The result is an agent that forgets what it found, states values it never computed or acts without knowing where to look. Given the same context, agents fail differently: one checks every source, another answers without looking, and a third gives up partway ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1: Same context, different agents (illustration). Given the same question and data, an investigator checks every source and answers from the data, a premature answerer answers without looking, and an early stopper gives up partway. Figure 2: Data agents and the context-engineering techniques that help them. Data agents answer questions over heterogeneous data, and context-engineering techniques (CETs) help by shaping the context the model works from: a semantic layer describes the data, orchestration splits the work and compaction condenses the history. What we do not yet know is how each changes what different LLMs do, alone and combined. Context engineering designs what an LLM conditions on at each step ( Mei et al., 2025 ) . Three context-engineering techniques (CETs) target these problems ( Figure 2 B). A semantic layer supplies a curated description of the data ( Sequeda et al., 2024 ; Rumiantsau and Fokeev, 2026 ; Chong et al., 2026 ) . Orchestration distributes work among a planner and specialist agents, each with its own context ( Wu et al., 2023 ) . Compaction replaces the growing history with a bounded working memory ( Packer et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) . Each is usually studied alone, in a setting built for it, and judged by its average accuracy effect, although all three edit the same finite prompt ( Section 5 ). Such studies tell whether a CET helps, but not what it changes in how an agent works, for which models or when CETs meet. Practitioners need to know which failure their agent has, which CET repairs it and when it breaks. Asked the question in Figure 1 , GPT-5.4 opens the file that answers it and replies São Paulo; given a semantic layer naming that file and saying to verify values with tools, it repeatedly replies “Lima” without any tool, as if the layer gave it the answer. GPT-5.5 answers which of four exchanges had the highest average market value among mining firms in 5-7 calls; with compaction it records the same answer by call nine, then “verifies” it for about 300 more actions. Alone, GPT-6 Astra correctly answers in four calls whether any metro area had more identity-theft than fraud reports; with orchestration, its verifier refuses a table labeled “Fraud and Other” as a stand-in for fraud and after 41 calls reports the question cannot be determined. Such cases raise four research questions (RQs; Figure 2 B-C). RQ1 : How do LLMs behave and fail as data agents without CETs? RQ2 : Does each CET help every model, and at what cost? RQ3 : What does each CET change in how an agent works: does a semantic layer make it look at the data (inspect it with tools) or stop looking, does orchestration make it investigate or box a strong one in, and does compaction save context and money or lose what was found? RQ4 : Do CETs add up? We study these questions where CETs are pushed to their limits: long-horizon tasks whose evidence is spread over files, databases, documents and the web, where the agent must choose what to inspect. Each CET is switched on or off on top of a baseline agent , a single tool-using agent with a growing context, and we test all eight combinations with seven LLMs on five benchmarks (1,514 tasks), with model, tools, limits and prompt fixed. A CET’s effect is not a property of the CET but of its match with the agent’s behavior: the same CET can rescue one model and degrade another, and what it was designed to improve, such as tool use, calls and prompt size, can improve while answers get worse. Orchestration gives models that answer before looking 23 points at four times the cost; the layer gives models that give up a larger gain than orchestration at a fraction of its cost; compaction cuts their give-ups on the longest tasks; and no CET raises the accuracy of agents that already investigate. Choosing a CET is thus a question about the agent, not a default. Our contributions are: (1) a controlled evaluation of data agents under every combination of semantic layers, orchestration and compaction, which prior work evaluates one at a time, measuring accuracy, behavior, cost and each benchmark’s process measures; (2) a behavioral analysis of every run’s trace that sorts the seven LLMs into three behavior groups and shows that each CET helps the groups whose habit it repairs while harming the investigators, and that combined CETs yield smaller gains and losses than their sum; (3) an analysis of wrong answers showing that selecting the wrong slice of data remains the most common cause after the agent inspects the data, under every combination of CETs; and (4) practical guidance for choosing and combining CETs by agent behavior, task demands and the accuracy-cost trade-off.

sections.heading: 2 Framework
sections.text: An agent answers a question by acting on files, databases, documents and, where allowed, the web. Switching each CET on or off on top of a baseline agent gives eight configurations that share the same model, tools, decoding settings and budget of steps and calls ( Figure 2 B; Appendix A ).

sections.heading: Baseline agent.
sections.text: A single tool-using agent ( Yao et al., 2022 ) . At each step it writes a thought and issues one action (Python, SQL, a file operation, or a web or document search), observes the result and decides what to do next, until it answers. It therefore already plans, inspects any source, tests intermediate results with code and corrects its course when an action fails or a result looks wrong. Its prompt tells it that computed values must come from executed code over the data, not from the question’s wording, and to keep working until it has computed the answer. The CETs do not add functions the baseline agent lacks; they change its context and how its work is organized.

sections.heading: Semantic layer.
sections.text: A description of the data, written offline once per benchmark by an LLM from the data, with no answers or task-specific hints. For every source it records the ontology (what the source, its tables and columns are), the data profile (value samples, units, missing values, parsing recipes) and the contextualization (join keys, related sources, ambiguous names). The entries most relevant to the question go into the prompt before the first step, and the agent must verify them.

sections.heading: Orchestration.
sections.text: A planner without tools splits the question into subtasks and delegates them to specialist agents for files, Python, SQL, or web and document search. Each uses the baseline agent’s tools in its own context and returns a condensed result. A verifier accepts each result or sends the work back. With the layer on, the planner passes the relevant entries to each specialist.

sections.heading: Compaction.
sections.text: The agent carries a bounded working memory instead of the full history, rewritten after every step: the goal, what is done, computed values with their evidence and open items.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We use five benchmarks with 1,514 tasks in total, counting FDABench’s report and choice tasks as two. KramaBench ( Lai et al., 2026 ) (104 tasks) asks questions over data lakes of many files with irregular layouts. DataClaw ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) (492 tasks) poses consulting questions over noisy enterprise tables and policy texts with entity names in two languages, scored by an LLM judge. FDABench ( Wang et al., 2026 ) joins a database with documents and web evidence, as 218 report tasks scored by a rubric and 320 multiple-choice tasks. HybridDeepResearch (HDR; Wu et al. 2026 ; 380 tasks) gives the agent no schema (it must discover tables by querying) and chains clues across the database and the web.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5 and GPT-6 Astra ( OpenAI, 2026a ; OpenAI, 2026b ; OpenAI, 2026c ) , Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 ( Anthropic, 2026a ; Anthropic, 2026b ) , Gemini 2.5 Flash ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) and the open-weight GLM-4.7-Flash ( Zeng et al., 2025 ) , served locally, at provider defaults ( Appendix C ); GPT-5.5 wrote the layers.

sections.heading: Metrics and analysis.
sections.text: Accuracy is each benchmark’s own score ( Appendix L ). Cost is dollars per task at list prices ( Appendix K ). A CET’s effect is the change when it is switched on, averaged over the settings of the other two. Accuracy effects are in percentage points with 95% bootstrap intervals over tasks, and group effects average their models.

sections.heading: Behavior.
sections.text: From each run’s trace ( Appendices B and D ) we measure: Acts , runs at least one tool; Answer grounded ( Grounded ), the submitted value appears in a tool output; Covers sources ( Coverage ), share of needed source types touched; Persists , three or more actions; Recovers , share of failed calls followed by a success; No repeats , no identical action twice; Flags uncertainty ( Hedges ), a hedged answer (annotated by an LLM); No give-up , does not end saying no relevant data exists; Answers , ends with an answer; and Long loops , 100 or more model calls.

sections.heading: 4 Results
sections.text: We answer the research questions in turn: how the models behave as baseline agents (RQ1, Section 4.1 ), whether each CET helps every model (RQ2, Section 4.2 ), what each changes in how an agent works (RQ3, Sections 4.3 , 4.4 and 4.5 ) and whether the three add up (RQ4, Section 4.6 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Three Groups of Baseline Agents
sections.text: Under identical tools and instructions, the seven baseline agents fall into three behavior groups, investigators , premature answerers and early stoppers , which clustering recovers exactly ( Figure 3 ). Investigators lead every benchmark ( Table 1 ). For each group, our analyses rule out the obvious explanation. Investigators’ accuracy advantage is linked to grounding. Opus, Sonnet and Astra act in almost every run, ground most answers in tool outputs and rarely give up. Their edge is not knowledge: overall, answers without any tool are right in 7% of runs, against 44% after looking ( Appendix B ). Premature answering can persist despite reasoning. GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.4 often reply without any tool (on 54% and 24% of tasks), although the prompt tells them to compute from the data. When GPT-5.5 does act, its accuracy is more than twice as high, so this is a habit, not a lack of ability or of thought: more reasoning does not reliably remove it, while orchestration, which demands evidence, does ( Appendices C and 4.3 ). Early stoppers abandon solvable tasks despite substantial effort. Gemini and GLM act, but give up with “no relevant data” in about 15% of runs and repeat an identical action in 28-29%. They do not give up for lack of data or effort: when they do, they have usually touched every source type the task needs, after three times as many actions as an investigator’s typical run, and at least one investigator solves 80% of those tasks ( Appendix D ). After looking, all groups fail alike, mostly by selecting the wrong data slice or misreading documents and web evidence, rarely by arithmetic, and no CET removes these causes ( Figure 14 ). sections.heading: 4.2 CET Benefits Depend on Agent Behavior and Task Demands
sections.text: Every CET costs more, and what it returns depends on the group. Orchestration and the semantic layer help the weaker groups ( Figure 4 ). For premature answerers, orchestration gives the largest gain we measure, 23 points, at four times the dollars. For early stoppers, the layer is cheaper and gives them over twice orchestration’s gain (4.6 against 1.8 points), at 1.1 rather than 2.3 times the dollars. Compaction does its job, keeping every prompt small, and pays off where history grows longest; averaged over tasks it changes accuracy by at most two points. The strongest models are where the expectation fails: for investigators, every CET lowers accuracy or leaves it unchanged, at a higher cost. CETs built to help an agent with its context make the strongest models worse. Figure 4: Accuracy-cost trade-offs depend on the behavior group. Each arrow goes from the baseline agent (square) to the agent with one CET: accuracy change in points and dollars per task as a multiple of the baseline’s. Orchestration gives the largest gain for premature answerers and the semantic layer for early stoppers; for investigators every CET lowers accuracy or leaves it unchanged, and every CET raises the cost. Figure 5: Task demands modify CET effects, and process gains can accompany accuracy losses. Rows show each CET’s effect on accuracy (overall and within-benchmark contrasts between tasks with and without each demand), process score (the mean of three benchmarks’ step scores), and dollars per task. Blue indicates improvement and red degradation; white marks effects below the display thresholds of one accuracy point, three process-score points, and 1.1 times the cost. Figure 16 reports every demand, each benchmark’s process measure, and which changes are significant. Each CET also responds to a different side of the task. LLMs label what each task demands, such as an under-specified question, small data or a long task, and we compare tasks with and without each demand within a benchmark ( Figure 5 ; Appendix E ). Orchestration responds to the question: it loses accuracy when the question is under-specified, as orchestrated agents stop stating the assumptions it needs. The layer responds to the data: it helps most on small, lightly messy data, and less when three or four sources must be combined. Compaction responds to the length of the work: its effect depends on task length ( Section 4.5 ), and the longest tasks also shrink the other CETs’ gains. Process scores can rise while accuracy falls. The benchmarks’ process scores, the share of expected steps a run takes, rise most with orchestration ( Figure 5 ), but do not tell whether answers improve: orchestration raises investigators’ process score by 11 points while their accuracy falls by 5. Neither shows how an agent works, so we measure behavior ( Figures 6 and 17 ), in three blocks: engagement (Acts, Coverage, Persists), reliability (Grounded, No give-up, No repeats, Long loops, Recovers) and commitment (Answers, Flags uncertainty). Behavior shows what the scores hide. Orchestration raises engagement, most for premature answerers, who act, cover sources and persist in 36-50 points more runs, and its cost falls on commitment, which neither score sees: investigators, whose process score rises while their accuracy falls, flag uncertainty and end with an answer less often, as do the early stoppers. The layer raises reliability at the expense of engagement: runs repeat and loop less in every group but persist less, so investigators’ unchanged scores hide that they look less. Compaction barely changes either score but adds repeated actions in all groups. A CET helps when it changes the behavior the agent lacks; otherwise it changes the agent without improving it. Figure 6: How each CET changes what agents do. For each group, a line outside the dashed ring means the CET makes a behavior more common and a line inside it less common; behaviors are grouped into engagement, reliability and commitment. Orchestration raises engagement, the semantic layer raises reliability at the cost of engagement, and compaction lowers reliability; Figure 17 gives every measure.

sections.heading: 4.3 Orchestration Helps Premature Answerers but Can Harm Investigators
sections.text: Orchestration delivers what it promises. The agent uses more tools, reaches more sources and persists longer, and for premature answerers this pays off: GPT-5.5 gains 37-47 points on benchmarks where it often answers without a tool. The gain is largest where the baseline agent is weakest, as Kim et al. (2025) also find, but it follows the habit more than the weakness: GPT-5.5 and Gemini start from similar accuracy (21% and 25%), yet orchestration gives GPT-5.5 35 points and Gemini less than one, because GPT-5.5 does not look and Gemini does ( Appendix E ). The gain is not a larger budget. A single GPT-5.5 agent forced to act before answering, or to spend as many calls as orchestration, closes at most 37% of the gap ( Figure 19 ): it runs one action, then repeats the answer it gave before looking. What orchestration adds is structure: a planner that asks for evidence, and specialists that must return it. Orchestration also has a cost. For investigators, it lowers accuracy by 5 points at 1.7 times the dollars, mostly on tasks that chain a database with documents and web search (6-12 points), and not for lack of data: it usually reaches every needed source ( Appendix G ). It changes how an answer is judged and stated. The verifier approves 87% of the investigators’ wrong answers, or, for Astra, rejects usable evidence until the planner abstains on 15.5% of HDR tasks, and investigators hedge far less. Orchestration makes a careful agent more confident and less thorough. Figure 7: The semantic layer cuts give-ups, long loops and calls, but raises the bill and makes investigators stop looking. It helps most the agents that give up, halving their give-ups and loops at little extra cost. Investigators instead stop using tools on most runs whose tool use changes, and their accuracy there falls from 68% to 31%.

sections.heading: 4.4 Semantic Layers Help Early Stoppers but Can Discourage Investigation
sections.text: For the weaker groups, the layer works. The semantic layer is built to help in three ways: the ontology says what each source is, the data profile how to read it, and the contextualization how sources relate. It names candidate sources, contains no answers and tells the agent to check every entry. It works as built ( Figure 7 ): told that an answer exists and where it lives, the models that give up most halve their give-ups on DataClaw, and early stoppers ground more answers and loop less. Each part does what it is built for ( Appendix H ): with the ontology, agents open the source it lists first in 27-42% of runs, against 4-13%; with the data profile, 16-20 points fewer runs fail to read a file; and the contextualization’s join keys are used where joins are needed. Fewer calls do not mean lower cost. A layer is also expected to make an agent cheaper, and every group needs 22-30% fewer calls; but the layer is in every prompt, so dollars rise 1.1-1.9 times, and only for the early stoppers is the gain nearly free. The layer also has a side effect: told what the data contains, the investigators look less. Opus stops using tools in 73 runs where its baseline agent used them and starts in only 11, and on the investigators’ runs that stop looking, accuracy falls from 68% to 31%. The layer is rarely wrong: of 100 investigator answers that went from right to wrong with the layer, it misled the agent in 2, while in 25 the agent stopped checking. Nor does the writer matter much: a layer written by a 3B model gives nearly the same gain as one by GPT-5.5 ( Figure 24 ). The layer is a guide, and the investigators treat it as the answer. If a layer correctly says a sales table lists a price per product, for instance, the agent reads that column and answers, where without the layer it would open the table and notice a second column of discounted prices. Although told to verify every entry, they stop checking, the checking that sets them apart ( Appendix H ). For an agent that looks too little the layer is a map; for one that already looks, it replaces looking ( Chong et al., 2026 , cf.) . sections.heading: 4.5 Compaction Bounds Context but Can Increase Cost and Repetition
sections.text: Compaction delivers the benefit it is known for. Each prompt stays near three times the size of the first prompt ( Figure 8 ), whereas without compaction the full transcript grows to fourteen times. GLM-4.7-Flash, with its short context window, no longer has to truncate its history when it orchestrates. The working memory keeps what matters: after every DataClaw rewrite, most models kept 92-100% of computed values. Its accuracy effect depends on task length. Where the history grows longest, compaction does most for the agents that lose track of it: on tasks that take other models longest, the early stoppers give up less and do 2.5 points better than on their other tasks, and GPT-5.4 gives up less. On short tasks, with little to compress, early stoppers lose 8 points, as each rewrite risks losing what was found. It also has costs: a smaller prompt is not a smaller bill. Every step adds a call that rewrites the memory, so total input barely changes (4-17% more tokens) while output, the costliest token, grows 2.3 to 3.5 times, and dollars rise 1.2 to 1.8 times. And some agents loop. A model that distrusts its result keeps checking it: 81% of premature answerers’ repeats re-check a value still in memory, and 42% of GPT-5.5’s DataClaw runs reach 100 or more calls (none without it) at eight times the cost.

sections.heading: 4.6 Combining CETs Offers Limited Added Gains but Can Mitigate Harms
sections.text: Combined effects are smaller than the sum of their parts. One might expect CETs to help each other, each fixing what others miss. For accuracy they mostly do not ( Table 2 ): they fix the same behaviors, so each helps less when another is on, and their harms do not add up either ( Appendix J ). Each pair shows a different side of this. The layer adds little to orchestration. The layer and orchestration both help agents find data. One might expect the layer to make orchestration cheaper, since its specialists search less, and they make fewer calls; but every prompt carries the layer, so the cost rises while accuracy barely does. Orchestration and compaction combine worst. Under orchestration, compaction makes more runs loop (10 more points of runs reach 100 or more calls, against 6 without it) and cuts orchestration’s gain in grounded answers from +12 to +4 points. The layer and compaction work well together. Compaction rewrites the agent’s memory after every step, which makes runs loop and lose grounding; the layer is not part of that memory, and with it compaction’s rise in long runs falls from 9 to 6 points, its multiplier on calls from 4.1 to 3.0, and under orchestration its drop in grounded answers from 6 points to under 1, most for models that loop most. The layer thus combines best: it adds little where another CET already fixes the same habit, but makes compaction cheaper and safer. In practice, a second CET should repair what the first leaves. Start with the CET matching the agent’s habit, and add another only for a habit it leaves or a behavior it causes: leave an agent that looks alone; give one that does not orchestration, plus a layer if it also gives up; use compaction for long runs, with the layer. sections.heading: Data agent benchmarks.
sections.text: LLM evaluation on data has moved from one query over one database ( Lei et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) to agents that find, read and combine evidence across data lakes of irregular files ( Lai et al., 2026 ) , enterprise tables and policy texts ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , databases joined with documents and the web ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , and heterogeneous workspaces ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Even strong agents are far from reliable ( Jing et al., 2025 ) : the best published KramaBench agent scores 56%, humans 77% ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . They also trace part of the difficulty to how agents behave, not what they can reach: giving an agent only the gold files raises KramaBench accuracy by 0-7% ( Lai et al., 2026 ) , DataClaw finds models stopping early on tasks they fail ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and reasoning models can cost more without answering better ( Wang et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Context-engineering techniques.
sections.text: A line of work adds techniques that manage what the model sees. A semantic layer describes the data, and such descriptions raise the accuracy of question answering over databases ( Sequeda et al., 2024 ; Rumiantsau and Fokeev, 2026 ; Somayajula et al., 2026 ) ; schema selection helps weaker text-to-SQL models in particular ( Maamari et al., 2024 ) . Orchestration splits the work among agents with their own contexts ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Hadfield et al., 2025 ) and helps most when the single agent is weak ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . Compaction bounds the history and, with optimized or trained compression, keeps accuracy at lower peak token use ( Packer et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) . The same studies report limits, mostly for strong models: schema selection and a static semantic layer can lower the accuracy of capable models ( Maamari et al., 2024 ; Chong et al., 2026 ) , a single agent given the same budget can match a multi-agent system ( Tran and Kiela, 2026 ) , and plain summaries are no better than dropping old observations ( Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) . The closest studies relate orchestration’s benefit to the single agent’s strength ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and compare ways of delivering a semantic layer ( Chong et al., 2026 ) ; both judge by accuracy. We study the CETs together across seven LLMs and describe each by the behavior it changes and the failures it repairs, relative to the agent’s habits.

sections.heading: 6 Practical Guidance and Conclusion
sections.text: Context-engineering techniques are usually judged by their average effect; our results show that what they do depends on the agent’s habits. The same CET can rescue one agent and hurt another, and it can hurt while the measures it was built to improve, tool use, calls, prompt size and the benchmarks’ process scores, look better. The agents most at risk are the strongest: given a semantic layer, investigators treat it as the answer and stop checking, and under orchestration they hedge less and approve wrong answers. What helps weaker agents is not more compute but the CET that matches their habit: orchestration, which demands evidence, for agents that answer without looking, and a semantic layer for agents that give up. Compaction keeps prompts small but not the bill, and is safest with a layer, which keeps compacted runs from looping. None of the three fixes the most common remaining failure, choosing the wrong data after looking, which is where work on data agents should turn next.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our study covers seven LLMs from four providers, from frontier models to a small open-weight model served locally, under all eight combinations of three CETs on five benchmarks. Models change quickly, and newer ones may show behaviors beyond the three groups we observe; the behavioral measures we use make it straightforward to place a new model among them, and extending the study to more models and model families is a natural next step. We study three widely used CETs, each in one representative design. Context engineering also includes other techniques, and other designs of the ones we study. Our aim is not to cover them all but to show that CETs interact with the agent’s behavior and with each other in ways their average effects do not reveal; applying the same behavioral lens to other techniques and designs is promising future work. Our tasks ask agents to answer questions over heterogeneous and messy data from files, databases, documents and the web. Other domains, such as mathematical reasoning or software engineering, place different demands on agents, and whether the same behavior groups and interactions appear there is an interesting question for future work. Finally, we evaluate CETs as fixed configurations; systems that choose or adapt CETs to an agent’s observed behavior, which our results suggest could pay off, are a direction for future work.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Our study evaluates context-engineering techniques for data agents, not their readiness for autonomous deployment. We find that the same technique can improve one model while degrading another, and that reduced cost or increased tool use does not necessarily imply more accurate answers. Semantic layers can encourage unsupported conclusions, compaction can omit relevant evidence, and orchestration can propagate errors or introduce unnecessary computation. These failures could have serious consequences when analytical outputs inform medical, legal, financial, or other high-stakes decisions. Such applications require task-specific validation, traceable evidence, and appropriate human oversight. Agents accessing files, databases, or web sources should also operate with least-privilege permissions and safeguards against unintended disclosure or modification of data. Finally, our behavioral groupings describe patterns observed under the evaluated tasks and configurations, rather than fixed properties of models. We encourage practitioners to validate context-engineering choices against answer correctness and evidence provenance, rather than relying on aggregate benchmark gains or efficiency measures alone.
