Each prompt stays near three times the size of the first prompt ( Figure 8 ), whereas without compaction the full transcript grows to fourteen times. GLM-4.7-Flash, with its short context window, no longer has to truncate its history when it orchestrates. The working memory keeps what matters: after every DataClaw rewrite, most models kept 92-100% of computed values. Its accuracy effect depends on task length. Where the history grows longest, compaction does most for the agents that lose track of it: on tasks that take other models longest, the early stoppers give up less and do 2.5 points better than on their other tasks, and GPT-5.4 gives up less. On short tasks, with little to compress, early stoppers lose 8 points, as each rewrite risks losing what was found. It also has costs: a smaller prompt is not a smaller bill. Every step adds a call that rewrites the memory, so total input barely changes (4-17% more tokens) while output, the costliest token, grows 2.3 to 3.5 times, and dollars rise 1.2 to 1.8 times. And some agents loop. A model that distrusts its result keeps checking it: 81% of premature answerers’ repeats re-check a value still in memory, and 42% of GPT-5.5’s DataClaw runs reach 100 or more calls (none without it) at eight times the cost. 4.6 Combining CETs Offers Limited Added Gains but Can Mitigate Harms Combined effects are smaller than the sum of their parts. One might expect CETs to help each other, each fixing what others miss. For accuracy they mostly do not ( Table 2 ): they fix the same behaviors, so each helps less when another is on, and their harms do not add up either ( Appendix J ). Each pair shows a different side of this. The layer adds little to orchestration. The layer and orchestration both help agents find data. One might expect the layer to make orchestration cheaper, since its specialists search less, and they make fewer calls; but every prompt carries the layer, so the cost rises while accuracy barely does. Orchestration and compaction combine worst. Under orchestration, compaction makes more runs loop (10 more points of runs reach 100 or more calls, against 6 without it) and cuts orchestration’s gain in grounded answers from +12 to +4 points. The layer and compaction work well together. Compaction rewrites the agent’s memory after every step, which makes runs loop and lose grounding; the layer is not part of that memory, and with it compaction’s rise in long runs falls from 9 to 6 points, its multiplier on calls from 4.1 to 3.0, and under orchestration its drop in grounded answers from 6 points to under 1, most for models that loop most. The layer thus combines best: it adds little where another CET already fixes the same habit, but makes compaction cheaper and safer. In practice, a second CET should repair what the first leaves. Start with the CET matching the agent’s habit, and add another only for a habit it leaves or a behavior it causes: leave an agent that looks alone; give one that does not orchestration, plus a layer if it also gives up; use compaction for long runs, with the layer. LLM evaluation on data has moved from one query over one database ( Lei et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) to agents that find, read and combine evidence across data lakes of irregular files ( Lai et al., 2026 ) , enterprise tables and policy texts ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , databases joined with documents and the web ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , and heterogeneous workspaces ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Even strong agents are far from reliable ( Jing et al., 2025 ) : the best published KramaBench agent scores 56%, humans 77% ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . They also trace part of the difficulty to how agents behave, not what they can reach: giving an agent only the gold files raises KramaBench accuracy by 0-7% ( Lai et al., 2026 ) , DataClaw finds models stopping early on tasks they fail ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and reasoning models can cost more without answering better ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Context-engineering techniques. A line of work adds techniques that manage what the model sees. A semantic layer describes the data, and such descriptions raise the accuracy of question answering over databases ( Sequeda et al., 2024 ; Rumiantsau and Fokeev, 2026 ; Somayajula et al., 2026 ) ; schema selection helps weaker text-to-SQL models in particular ( Maamari et al., 2024 ) . Orchestration splits the work among agents with their own contexts ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Hadfield et al., 2025 ) and helps most when the single agent is weak ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . Compaction bounds the history and, with optimized or trained compression, keeps accuracy at lower peak token use ( Packer et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) . The same studies report limits, mostly for strong models: schema selection and a static semantic layer can lower the accuracy of capable models ( Maamari et al., 2024 ; Chong et al., 2026 ) , a single agent given the same budget can match a multi-agent system ( Tran and Kiela, 2026 ) , and plain summaries are no better than dropping old observations ( Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) . The closest studies relate orchestration’s benefit to the single agent’s strength ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and compare ways of delivering a semantic layer ( Chong et al., 2026 ) ; both judge by accuracy. We study the CETs together across seven LLMs and describe each by the behavior it changes and the failures it repairs, relative to the agent’s habits. 6 Practical Guidance and Conclusion Context-engineering techniques are usually judged by their average effect; our results show that what they do depends on the agent’s habits. The same CET can rescue one agent and hurt another, and it can hurt while the measures it was built to improve, tool use, calls, prompt size and the benchmarks’ process scores, look better. The agents most at risk are the strongest: given a semantic layer, investigators treat it as the answer and stop checking, and under orchestration they hedge less and approve wrong answers. What helps weaker agents is not more compute but the CET that matches their habit: orchestration, which demands evidence, for agents that answer without looking, and a semantic layer for agents that give up. Compaction keeps prompts small but not the bill, and is safest with a layer, which keeps compacted runs from looping. None of the three fixes the most common remaining failure, choosing the wrong data after looking, which is where work on data agents should turn next. Limitations Our study covers seven LLMs from four providers, from frontier models to a small open-weight model served locally, under all eight combinations of three CETs on five benchmarks. Models change quickly, and newer ones may show behaviors beyond the three groups we observe; the behavioral measures we use make it straightforward to place a new model among them, and extending the study to more models and model families is a natural next step. We study three widely used CETs, each in one representative design. Context engineering also includes other techniques, and other designs of the ones we study. Our aim is not to cover them all but to show that CETs interact with the agent’s behavior and with each other in ways their average effects do not reveal; applying the same behavioral lens to other techniques and designs is promising future work. Our tasks ask agents to answer questions over heterogeneous and messy data from files, databases, documents and the web. Other domains, such as mathematical reasoning or software engineering, place different demands on agents, and whether the same behavior groups and interactions appear there is an interesting question for future work. Finally, we evaluate CETs as fixed configurations; systems that choose or adapt CETs to an agent’s observed behavior, which our results suggest could pay off, are a direction for future work. Ethical Considerations Our study evaluates context-engineering techniques for data agents, not their readiness for autonomous deployment. We find that the same technique can improve one model while degrading another, and that reduced cost or increased tool use does not necessarily imply more accurate answers. Semantic layers can encourage unsupported conclusions, compaction can omit relevant evidence, and orchestration can propagate errors or introduce unnecessary computation. These failures could have serious consequences when analytical outputs inform medical, legal, financial, or other high-stakes decisions. Such applications require task-specific validation, traceable evidence, and appropriate human oversight. Agents accessing files, databases, or web sources should also operate with least-privilege permissions and safeguards against unintended disclosure or modification of data. Finally, our behavioral groupings describe patterns observed under the evaluated tasks and configurations, rather than fixed properties of models. We encourage practitioners to validate context-engineering choices against answer correctness and evidence provenance, rather than relying on aggregate benchmark gains or efficiency measures alone. Six describe the data: the modalities involved (tabular files, SQL database, text documents, document corpus, web search, specialized formats, media), the SQL dialect, the number of sources needed, how the source must be found (given, small pool, large file pool), the cross-source step (none, relational join, entity matching, database-web or document bridge) and the data scale. Appendix C Reasoning Effort All main runs use provider defaults, under which every model reasons except GPT-5.4 (the Claude models use adaptive thinking, which Claude Opus 5.5 cannot turn off; Anthropic, 2026a ; Anthropic, 2026b ). To see whether answering before looking is a setting or a habit, we ran the baseline agent of both models on KramaBench (104 tasks) and HDR (380 tasks) at other reasoning efforts: low and high for GPT-5.5, medium and high for GPT-5.4 ( Figure 12 ). Everything else is unchanged. In the figure, the orange bars fall and the blue bars rise for GPT-5.4 as effort grows, while both stay nearly flat for GPT-5.5. For GPT-5.4, reasoning removes the habit. Its share of tasks answered without a tool falls from 24% to 8% (medium) and 3% (high) on KramaBench, and from 32% to 7% and 3% on HDR. Its accuracy rises by 35 points on KramaBench (.37 to .72 and .70; +35.1 [+25.1, +44.6] at medium, 57 tasks better and 8 worse) and by 35-36 points on HDR (.08 to .43 and .45; 157-162 tasks better, 16-17 worse). Both values exceed the best of its eight configurations without reasoning (.63 and .23). The cost per task rises from $0.07 to $0.18-$0.21 on KramaBench and from $0.10 to $0.53-$0.66 on HDR, about what orchestration costs it. For GPT-5.5, more reasoning moves the habit only a little. At high effort it still answers without a tool on 78% of KramaBench and 87% of HDR tasks (89% and 94% at the default), and its accuracy does not change clearly (+4.3 [ − - 2.1, +11.3] and +0.2 [ − - 2.4, +2.9] points). Low effort raises the share without a tool to 96% and 98%. When it does act at high effort, its accuracy is again more than twice as high (.49 against .20 on KramaBench). Answering before looking therefore has two forms, with two different remedies. In GPT-5.4 it comes with reasoning switched off, and switching reasoning on gives a larger gain than orchestration at about the same cost. In GPT-5.5 it persists at every effort: more thinking does not make the model look, and only orchestration, which asks for evidence from outside the model, does ( Section 4.3 ). Reasoning and orchestration are therefore not interchangeable ways of spending more compute; which one helps depends on why the agent does not look.
